title: Homeless by Choice
dek: In Seattle, a person can eat, wash, get online, receive medical care and sometimes sleep without paying a bill. What does that make possible—and what kind of freedom does it buy?
body: At Edible Hope Kitchen in Ballard, Friday means pancakes and eggs. The meal costs nothing. St. Luke’s Episcopal Church’s program currently serves from the basement of St. Paul’s United Church of Christ, from eight to ten each weekday morning. Its published menu includes a protein dish, starch, coffee and oatmeal; other days can bring curry, meatloaf or salmon. This is an actual place to eat, with an address and a schedule. Any serious argument about choosing homelessness in Seattle has to begin there.

It should continue at the food bank, the library and the shower. Ballard Food Bank provides groceries, meals and bags designed for people without cooking facilities. Urban Rest Stop offers washing, laundry and toiletries at no charge. Seattle Public Library supplies computers and internet access. Those provisions can remove expenses from a person’s life rather than merely make them cheaper.

The question is more unsettling when the person has no car to finance, no student loans and no other debt. Suppose a young adult can secure a place in an organized tent city or a tiny-house village, eat through a combination of benefits and donated meals, and get healthcare through Washington’s Medicaid program. Suppose the available alternative is an office job that pays the bills while consuming most of the week. What, exactly, is the financial incentive to return?

Seattle makes very low-cash living possible for some people. A private car, a broadband subscription and monthly rent can all disappear from the ledger. What remains depends on where the person sleeps, how they obtain food and care, and how much control they have over tomorrow. A tiny house, an organized camp and an exposed sidewalk produce radically different answers.
## The city that exists between the bills

Consider the practical geography. In Ballard, Edible Hope covers a weekday morning meal. The food bank’s Kindness Café operates Monday through Thursday, with longer hours on Tuesday and Thursday. Ballard Sunday Dinner lists a meal from five to six on Sunday evenings at Ballard First Lutheran Church. These are overlapping resources, rather than one institution promising every meal of every day.

There are other networks elsewhere in Seattle. Community Lunch on Capitol Hill lists weekday breakfast and lunch, welcomes anyone without a sign-in requirement, and distributes such items as coats, socks and sleeping bags. A person need not buy a restaurant meal simply because they lack a private kitchen.

Food banks also know that a bag of ingredients is not much use without a stove. Ballard’s no-cook provision addresses precisely that problem. Its resource hub offers a mailing address and help with identification, among other services. An apartment usually bundles these practical functions together; Seattle’s assistance network can supply several of them separately.

The library is equally significant. Someone using its computers need not own a laptop or pay for home internet. Public internet computers generally allow two hours daily with a card; guest passes provide a shorter session, and some job-search computers offer additional time. Wi-Fi is free during open hours. The library is a place to read, apply for work, handle paperwork and spend part of a wet day indoors. It is not necessary to turn each of those activities into a purchase.

St. Luke’s also advertises Sunday worship at ten. Faith, company and a recurring place in the week belong in the accounting, even if they cannot be assigned a dollar value. A church meal can connect someone with people who recognize them. A library can offer continuity. These are parts of a life, not just substitutions for consumer goods.

## A roof without a rent check

Free shelter is real. Washington 211 lists no fees for SHARE/WHEEL’s Tent Cities 3 and 4. Its descriptions also say there is no individual length-of-stay limit, subject to the programs’ rules. That matters: it is inaccurate to portray every organized camp as a single overnight stop from which a person must start over the next morning.

SHARE/WHEEL describes communities with resident governance, security, toilets, trash collection and a food-preparation area. Volunteers provide hot meals most evenings, and the organization lists daily bus tickets for participants. Residents help operate the camps. A camp can therefore reduce transport and storage costs as well as the cost of sleeping.

A tiny house changes the physical arrangement again. LIHI describes private, locking units with beds, storage, electricity and heating, with shared facilities in the village. This is a substantial improvement over trying to stay dry in a tent. A person in such a unit should not be written about as though they spend every night exposed to rain.

The routes into these places differ. LIHI works through outreach and referral partners and requires participation in case management. Nickelsville runs self-managed villages with its own intake process, interviews and participation obligations. Its Northlake procedure asks applicants to check whether interviews are taking place that week; its Central District procedure includes a meeting and a waitlist.

Washington 211’s detailed Nickelsville listings say there are no fees and describe shared kitchen, shower and laundry facilities. One directory summary still mentions utility fees. That inconsistency is a reason to verify a particular placement’s terms, not to invent a market rent for it. The correct budget entry is zero for an admitted resident of a genuinely no-fee program, with any actual charge stated separately.

The city’s need remains much larger than these examples. KCRHA’s initial 2026 count estimated 18,365 people experiencing homelessness across King County, including 11,829 unsheltered and 6,536 sheltered—an overall increase of nine percent from 2024. These are county figures, not a Seattle-only count, and they do not measure how many people voluntarily chose homelessness.

A free place can be a durable arrangement for one resident while remaining unavailable to the next applicant. Both facts belong in the story. A meal listing establishes a meal service. A village listing establishes a program. Neither establishes that an individual has secured a bed.
## The park is another column

People also camp in parks without paying rent. That belongs in a description of how Seattle homelessness actually works. It is different from admission to a sanctioned camp: the city’s published parks rules generally prohibit camping under SMC 18.12.250. A tent may be physically present without its occupant having permission to remain.

For the person, the rent can still be zero. Donated equipment can reduce the cost of setting up. The material difference is the lack of assured tenure, village facilities and organized support at the sleeping site. Weather exposure, moving possessions and possible removal belong in the analysis. Assigning those concerns an invented monthly bill would obscure them rather than measure them.

## Put the zeroes where they belong

For the comparison below, the person is an adult without children, a car or debt. The homeless scenario assumes that free shelter has already been obtained, eligible healthcare is active, and meals, donated supplies and public facilities meet the listed needs. This is a conditional cash budget, not a claim that every homeless Seattle resident spends the same amount.

The housed columns show a worker paying for ordinary goods and services. The solo housing, food and medical entries draw on MIT’s King County benchmarks; the shared room and smaller personal expenses are disclosed assumptions. Both housed examples use transit. Nobody is assigned a vehicle.

The low total in the third column follows directly from the assumptions. If the individual pays no rent, buys no groceries with cash, receives covered medical care and uses free hygiene facilities and internet, those particular cash costs can be zero. The EBT balance belongs on the benefits side of the ledger. Donated meals belong on the support side. The recipient does not pay their market value.

Nor should the comparison quietly load up the working person’s lifestyle. Housed people can use libraries and open meal programs, too. In the shared-housing example, eliminating the phone and home-internet allowances, purchased food, clothing, laundry and toiletries through the same assumed free resources reduces the modeled total from $2,042 to $1,466. That version still includes housing, the medical benchmark, full-price transit and renters insurance. It makes the comparison less dramatic and more honest.

Eligibility can narrow it further. A low-income worker may qualify for reduced fares or benefits. Employer transit subsidies can also change an individual’s result. Housing status alone does not determine benefit eligibility, and full-time work does not invariably produce the same package of costs.

To see the distinction between avoiding a bill and building wealth, give the shared-housing worker an illustrative $3,200 per month after tax, before the medical costs counted in the table. Subtract $2,042 and $1,158 remains. The person without wages and with a zero-cash arrangement has no rent bill, but also no earned cash surplus. If that person needs a $36 pass, the cash gap is $36. These are arithmetic examples, not typical incomes.

That does not settle the question in favor of the job. The worker has sold time to produce the surplus. The person outside paid employment may value time more highly than that surplus, especially if the work is exhausting or humiliating. But a fair comparison must show both money and time. It cannot call foregone rent “savings” while overlooking the wage that also disappeared.

A person with modest paid work and no rent occupies a third position. They may have cash for needs that donations do not cover while retaining much of the time gained by keeping expenses low. Earnings can change benefit amounts and eligibility, so the calculation must be made for that person. Homelessness and employment are not mutually exclusive.
## Real Change changes the arithmetic

Selling Real Change adds an income stream to this picture. The publisher’s current organization profile lists a vendor purchase price of $1.25 and a cover price of $4, with vendors also receiving tips. The difference is $2.75 per paper sold before other costs and taxes. That is work with a small inventory requirement, not simply a handout.

The distinction matters psychologically as well as financially. A vendor can have customers, familiar faces and a task they control without entering a conventional office. The question becomes whether modest, flexible earnings combined with free services can support a life the person prefers. Homelessness need not mean zero income.

Sales volumes are hypothetical, not reported averages."}

If 200 papers are purchased and all sell, the $550 trading margin leaves $514 after a $36 transit pass, before taxes, other business costs and personal purchases. Tips could increase receipts; unsold copies and expenses could reduce the result. To assess the hourly return, the reporting would need actual hours spent selling, obtaining papers and traveling. A monthly sales count alone cannot tell us the wage.

The sources checked do not establish how many Seattle homeless adults sell Real Change, what a new vendor typically earns, or how many vendors are Gen Z. A program’s existence does not guarantee a customer base. But newspaper sales make an important third possibility visible: earning money without accepting the schedule, hierarchy or expenses of a conventional office life.

Earnings also change the benefits analysis. The later SNAP figure is a maximum for someone meeting all requirements, not an automatic amount to add to every sales scenario. Self-employment income, allowable business expenses and applicable reporting rules must be evaluated. The feature therefore does not combine a vendor’s modeled margin with an assumed unchanged maximum EBT award.
## The EBT card is substantial—and conditional

Washington calls its SNAP program Basic Food. The federal maximum for a one-person household in the contiguous states is $306 per month for October 2026 through September 2027. That is $10.20 per day over a 30-day month in food purchasing power, not cash for any purpose. A maximum benefit is not every recipient’s award.

At zero countable income, an otherwise eligible household can receive the maximum. But the benefit cannot simply be treated as an indefinite allowance for every adult who prefers not to work. Washington’s current rules impose time limits on certain adults without dependents. DSHS lists paid work averaging 80 hours monthly, approved employment or training, or Workfare as ways to meet the requirement, with exemptions for qualifying circumstances. The rules apply statewide from February 2026.

Workfare is especially relevant to this story. Its required volunteer hours are calculated from the benefit amount and the applicable minimum wage; it is not automatically the same as an 80-hour paid-work requirement. A person can contribute outside an office. Ordinary volunteering, however, should not be assumed to count until the program confirms it.

For someone leaving a job, separate voluntary-quit rules can also affect food assistance when no accepted good cause applies. There are exemptions and individual determinations. “Quit, get an EBT card, and never deal with work again” is therefore an unreliable description of the system.

Free meals and food-bank assistance are separate resources. Losing SNAP does not automatically mean losing access to every charity meal. Equally, losing $306 in monthly food purchasing power is a meaningful loss even if a lunch line remains open. The story should neither erase the benefit nor exaggerate its permanence.
## Healthcare without the employer

Washington’s Apple Health program provides a real alternative to employer insurance for eligible low-income adults. It covers physical and behavioral healthcare, including mental-health services. For a qualifying person receiving covered care through the program, the appropriate comparison can be zero personal premium and zero covered-service charges—not an invented private insurance bill. Eligibility includes income and other program conditions; homelessness does not enroll someone automatically.

That changes the supposed bargain of employment. The worker who tolerates a miserable job chiefly for insurance may have another route to treatment. Medicaid coverage does not mean that a person must buy mental-health counseling at private-pay prices. It also does not guarantee an immediate appointment with any therapist they choose. Coverage, provider access and continuity of treatment are different questions.

The time horizon matters. HCA currently announces new work or community-engagement requirements for affected Apple Health for Adults enrollees beginning January 1, 2027, with exemptions and other ways to meet the rules. The agency also lists six-month renewals for this group. Those changes are prospective as of publication. They make a lifetime projection based only on today’s coverage rules particularly weak.

The accurate point is straightforward: healthcare and mental-health treatment can be publicly covered. Whether a particular person can keep that coverage, obtain the care they need and stay connected to providers must be examined rather than assumed.
## What the body pays

The physical comparison starts with where a person sleeps. A heated, locking tiny house provides protection and private space. An organized tent city adds shared facilities, security and community but still leaves more of daily life outside. Someone sleeping alone without either arrangement faces a different level of exposure and uncertainty. The same zero in a rent column cannot describe all three environments.

Access to showers, clean clothes, regular food and treatment can materially improve daily life. It is inaccurate to write as though every person without an apartment is necessarily dirty, hungry or medically abandoned. It is equally inaccurate to say that a library’s daytime warmth resolves the need for a dependable place to sleep.

There is strong reason to take health risks seriously without turning them into a scare story about one young adult. A national study following roughly 140,000 people identified as homeless in the 2010 Census found that nonelderly members of that group had about 3.5 times the mortality risk of housed people after adjustment for demographic and geographic differences. This is an observational comparison of a broad population, not a causal estimate of what will happen to a healthy person entering a Seattle tiny-house village.

The office worker’s body belongs in the story as well. Sleep lost to work, long periods sitting and the physical effects of stress are legitimate concerns to investigate. Yet “office job” is too broad a category to predict health. A reasonable schedule with supportive colleagues is a different exposure from chronic overwork under a threatening manager. Neither homelessness nor employment supplies one uniform physical experience.

For this particular comparison, the unanswered research question is more precise: how does the health of debt-free young adults who voluntarily live in well-supported Seattle communities change over time, compared with similar young adults in jobs they dislike? The sources reviewed here do not answer that question. General population mortality data cannot fill the gap.
## The mind, the schedule and the door

The psychological appeal of leaving can be rational. If rent drives the need for a job, and the job dominates waking life, removing the rent can feel like removing a threat. A person may gain time to read, make music, recover from exhaustion, attend appointments or simply stop performing enthusiasm.

The World Health Organization recognizes both sides of work: decent employment can provide purpose, routine and connection, while excessive demands, insecurity, bullying and low control can damage mental health. That supports taking an unhappy worker seriously. It does not establish that becoming homeless is a treatment, or that unemployment reliably improves well-being.

The alternative has a schedule of its own. Meals have serving windows. Laundry has sign-ups. Intake requires showing up. Camp responsibilities have to be completed. These tasks need not consume an entire day; bundling facilities in a village can reduce travel considerably. But hours released from employment are not automatically hours of uninterrupted leisure.

At Urban Rest Stop, a wash-and-dry cycle usually takes about an hour and a half. Someone using it four times monthly would spend roughly six hours in those cycles, some of which may overlap with a shower or other activity. That is a transparent time calculation, not a fabricated claim about average homeless “survival labor.” Travel and waiting would have to be measured separately.

Privacy is another form of control. A tiny house with a key offers more of it than a shared sleeping room. A public computer provides access without a bill, while a private connection offers different hours and discretion. A camp’s democratically chosen rules may feel more legitimate than an employer’s orders; they still govern what a resident can do.

These differences are often discussed as personal shortcomings. They are better understood as features of an arrangement: who sets the schedule, who can exclude someone, where possessions stay, and whether a disagreement threatens the place to sleep.
## The spiritual life outside the job title
The strongest evidence for community is not a romantic image of the street. It is what residents say about specific places.

In a You Know Me Now episode based on a January 2023 visit to Tent City 3, one resident called the camp “The family that I got to pick.” She described trust and emotional safety, said a layoff had made her homeless, and explained that she did not yet feel ready to leave the people there. Her account combines economic disruption with attachment and agency. It is not evidence that she entered homelessness as a career plan, or that she fits this article’s age and debt assumptions.

A 2026 study by Karen A. Snedker, Jennifer McKinney and Steven Pfaff gives that community dimension more substance. Drawing on interviews and observations across several waves from 2012 to 2025, the researchers examine Tent City 3’s self-government. They describe how shared responsibilities, resident voice and enforceable rules can generate social connection and personal agency. It is a case study, not a clinical trial or proof that every encampment works the same way.

There is a spiritual proposition here that deserves more than a sentimental paragraph: a person’s worth can be recognized through showing up, sharing food, caring for neighbors or helping govern a community. Salary and job title are not the only ways to become useful to other people.

For someone who experiences employment as a series of meaningless demands, that form of belonging may be powerful. A Sunday service, a familiar table or a security shift that protects someone you know can carry more personal meaning than another performance review. For someone else, worship may offer nothing and communal living may feel intrusive. Spiritual fulfillment is a question of experience, conviction and relationships, not a benefit issued automatically with a shelter placement.

Nor do these sources of meaning require homelessness. Housed workers can worship, volunteer, use libraries and build close relationships. The relevant comparison is whether the demands and costs of a particular working life leave enough time and energy to participate.
## The student loan that is not there

The young adult modeled here never went to college and owes no debt. Their student-loan payment is zero, whether they rent a room, enter a village or sell newspapers. This particular freedom from creditors is an assumption of the comparison, not a description of everyone experiencing homelessness.

Student debt matters as context for the generation’s choices. The New York Fed reported $1.65 trillion in outstanding student-loan balances in the second quarter of 2026, across borrowers of all ages. That total is not a Gen Z balance, and it does not describe the person modeled here.

For a separate borrower, $30,000 repaid at a fixed six percent over ten years would require about $333.06 a month and about $9,967 in interest, assuming standard monthly amortization with no subsidies or forgiveness. Those are illustrative calculations, not a statement of the prevailing loan rate or every borrower’s required payment.

Becoming homeless does not itself cancel that obligation. Federal income-driven repayment can change a payment according to the applicable plan and circumstances; the rules and available plans must be checked. The borrowed amount therefore belongs in a separate scenario, rather than being used to inflate a debt-free person’s cash needs.

The deeper question for someone who never borrowed is different. If they see education leading to debt and employment leading to rent, opting out may look like avoiding a sequence of commitments. That perception deserves examination. It does not establish that every degree is a bad investment, or that no-college workers lack careers worth having.
## Is it viable?

As a way to meet daily needs with very little personal cash, the arrangement is plausible under specific conditions. Seattle has documented programs that make it possible to eat, wash, connect to the internet, receive care and obtain shelter without paying market prices. Some organized communities offer more stability and belonging than the word “homeless” suggests.

As an alternative to a conventional job, the strongest version combines low cash needs with flexible earnings, such as newspaper sales. A vendor may cover personal expenses and accumulate some savings without paying market rent. The unanswered questions are whether sales are sufficient and dependable, whether benefits continue, and whether the person’s shelter arrangement lasts. The income-producing activity is a business; homelessness is the living arrangement around it.

The most consequential distinction is between a workable present and a reliable long-term option. An admitted resident with appropriate benefits, supportive relationships and a manageable set of duties may have a workable present. Someone who leaves housing on the assumption that the same resources will immediately become available has not yet secured that arrangement.

Calling all such choices irrational ignores how punishing low-paid work and rent can become. Calling the arrangement universally liberating ignores differences in health, safety, privacy, eligibility and access. Calling everyone who stays “homeless by choice” collapses distinct decisions: losing housing, declining an unsuitable shelter, valuing a camp community and rejecting paid employment are not interchangeable acts.

Seattle’s free services make the question possible. They also reveal what people need regardless of whether they hold a job: food, warmth, care, company and a place where they can belong. The test of a good life is larger than whether its bills add up to zero. So is the test of a good economy: it should be able to offer a young person something more convincing than an exhausting job whose principal reward is permission to remain indoors.
## Reporting and calculation notes

Reporting basis. This feature uses published reporting, program listings, official rules and research. No new interviews or firsthand observations were conducted. The main analytical case is a Seattle adult aged 19–29, without children, a car, college attendance or debt. That is a stipulated scenario, not a demographic claim about Seattle’s homeless population.

Reading the cost comparison. The tables distinguish cash paid by the individual from services and benefits supplied by others. A conditional zero means the specified need is met without personal cash in that scenario; it does not establish a measured average, an available vacancy, a guaranteed service or an adequate lifetime income. Benefits are not added to cash income.

Housing figures. The solo housing-and-utilities figure is MIT’s 2026 King County annual housing benchmark, $25,589, divided by 12 and rounded to $2,132. The shared figure is an editorial assumption: $1,000 rent plus $90 utilities. Neither is a current advertised rental offer. The shared utility allocation is $45 electricity/other energy and $45 water/sewer/garbage; lease arrangements vary.

Other housed costs. Food is MIT’s $5,234 annual benchmark divided by 12, rounded to $436; medical is $3,032 divided by 12, rounded to $253. These are modeled cost components, not quotes or a prescribed shopping basket. Transit is the published $108 monthly Metro pass. Phone, home internet, clothing, laundry, toiletries and renters insurance are explicit editorial allowances. These modified budgets are not MIT’s full living-wage budget. At the rounded monthly amounts, the food allowance is $100.62 per week when annualized over 52 weeks, or $14.53 per day in a 30-day month; the $253 medical line is an average allocation, not a bill expected every month. Actual employer premiums, copayments and deductibles vary.

Excluded from recurring totals. Taxes are handled by comparing costs with already-after-tax income; if health premiums are withheld from pay, add them back before comparing with a table that includes them. No childcare, pet costs, debt, car expenses, retirement contributions, emergency savings, entertainment or paid storage are included. Deposits, moving costs, device purchases and occasional uncovered needs are separate. Omitting a reserve does not make a future expense disappear.

Source conflicts. St. Luke’s meal program lists its current service at St. Paul’s, 8–10 a.m. weekdays; that operator listing takes precedence over older directories. SHARE/WHEEL’s current site lists Tent City locations that differ from older 211 addresses; location details here use the operator. Washington 211’s detailed Nickelsville listings say no fees, while one search-summary description mentions utility fees. The zero-fee tiny-house case is therefore conditional and any utility charge needs direct confirmation. No provider was contacted. Real Change’s updated publisher profile lists $1.25 wholesale/$4 retail; older directory pages return conflicting earlier prices. The publisher’s newer figures are used, and prices should be reconfirmed at publication.

Publication check. Program schedules, vacancies and benefit rules can change. Dates and limits below describe the sources checked on October 18, 2026. The 2027 Apple Health changes are identified as prospective. A reported profile would require additional consent-based interviews, including with young adults who actually fit the article’s voluntary, debt-free scenario. This feature does not invent such a person or claim to measure how common that choice is.

Vendor calculations. Paper-sales receipts are gross customer payments. Trading margin subtracts only purchased inventory, assuming all copies sell. It is not after-tax income. The budget table does not deduct hypothetical vendor income; the sales table shows it separately to avoid treating uncertain earnings or maximum benefits as guaranteed. No average sales rate or hourly wage is asserted.
